It is hung with golden threads; with necklaces, jeweled strings, diamond strings, bracelet strings, strings of red pearls and strings of blue pearls; decorated with lion creepers, girdles, bunches of jeweled cords and hundreds of jeweled coverings; weighed down with golden nets, pearl nets, nets of every jewel and nets of bangles; adorned with makaras, swastikas, nandyavarta coils and crescent moons; ornamented with little bells, gems, gold and every jewel ornament; and adorned according to the wishes and requests of beings.

And, Ananda, the sound that comes from that tree of awakening when the wind stirs it makes itself known in immeasurable worlds. There, Ananda, beings within whose hearing the sound of the tree of awakening comes need expect no disease of the ear until they reach awakening. Measureless, countless, inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, inexpressible beings within whose sight the tree of awakening comes need expect no disease of the eye until they reach awakening. And, Ananda, beings who smell the scent of that tree of awakening need never expect any disease of the nose until they reach awakening. Beings who taste the fruits of that tree of awakening need never expect any disease of the tongue until they reach awakening.

Beings touched by the light of that tree of awakening need never expect any disease of the body until they reach the seat of awakening. And, Ananda, beings who contemplate that tree of awakening in accordance with the Dharma need never expect any distraction of mind from then until they reach awakening. And all those beings, the moment they see that tree of awakening, stand firm in irreversibility from unsurpassed, perfect awakening, and gain the three acceptances: the acceptance that follows sound, the acceptance that conforms to the truth, and the acceptance that things are unborn. This is through the upholding power of the former vows of that very Tathagata Amitayus, because he did his service under the victors of the past, and because his former vows and practice were well completed, well developed, without lack or flaw.

And, Ananda, the bodhisattvas who have been born, are being born or will be born there are all bound to just one more birth, and will awaken right there to unsurpassed, perfect awakening; except, by the power of their vows, those bodhisattvas who have roared the great lion’s roar, who have put on the noble armor, and who are devoted to bringing all beings to final nirvana. And, Ananda, in that buddha-field the disciples shine with a light of a fathom, and the bodhisattvas with a light of a hundred thousand kotis of leagues; except for two bodhisattvas, by whose light that world is always and everywhere filled with constant radiance. Then the venerable Ananda said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, what are the names of those two good men, those bodhisattvas, great beings?”

The Blessed One said: “Ananda, one of the two is the bodhisattva, the great being, Avalokiteshvara, and the second is named Sthamaprapta (“One Who Has Gained Great Strength,” also called Mahasthamaprapta). Ananda, they passed away from this very buddha-field and were reborn there. And, Ananda, the bodhisattvas reborn in that buddha-field all have the thirty-two marks of a great person; their limbs are complete; they are skilled in the meditations and higher knowledges, skilled in the distinctions of wisdom; they are adept, with keen faculties, well-guarded faculties, faculties that understand, faculties neither feeble nor shaky; they have gained acceptance, and their good qualities are endless and boundless. And, Ananda, the bodhisattvas reborn in that buddha-field are never apart from seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma, and never fall into bad states, until they reach awakening.

And from then on none of them will ever fail to remember their former lives; except for those who, by an earlier vow, go into such turbulent eons, while the five corruptions are at work, when buddhas, blessed ones, appear in the world, as I do now. And, Ananda, the bodhisattvas reborn in that buddha-field all go to other worlds before a single morning meal and attend on many hundreds of thousands of kotis of nayutas of buddhas, as many as they wish. Through the Buddha’s power, as soon as they think, ‘Let us worship with such flowers, lamps, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, flags, banners, victory banners, instruments, songs and music,’ the moment the thought arises, just such means of worship appear in their hands.

Worshipping those buddhas, blessed ones, with those flowers and the rest, up to the music, they gather many, immeasurable, countless roots of goodness. And if they wish, ‘Let handfuls of flowers like this appear in our hands,’ the moment the thought arises, heavenly handfuls of flowers of many colors and many scents appear in their hands. With such handfuls of flowers they scatter, strew and shower those buddhas, blessed ones. And even the smallest handful of flowers they throw becomes a flower parasol ten leagues wide in the sky above; and the first does not fall to the ground before the second is thrown. Some handfuls of flowers, when thrown, become flower parasols twenty leagues wide in the sky above;

some thirty, forty or fifty, some a hundred thousand leagues wide appear in the sky above. There, those who feel great joy and gladness, and gain a great uplifting of the mind, plant many, immeasurable, countless roots of goodness, attend on many hundreds of thousands of kotis of nayutas of buddhas, and within that one morning are back again in the world Sukhavati; through the upholding and embrace of the former vows of that very Tathagata Amitayus, through the full and complete success of his former vows, without lack, well defined and well developed. And, Ananda, the bodhisattvas reborn in that buddha-field all give only talks on the Dharma that go together with all-knowing.

And in that buddha-field beings have no notion of possession at all. Walking about and wandering through the whole buddha-field, they feel neither delight nor discontent. When they leave, they leave without attachment, not with attachment; they have no such thought at all.

And, Ananda, the beings reborn in that world Sukhavati have no notion of ‘stranger,’ no notion of ‘one’s own,’ no notion of ‘mine’; there is no quarrel, no dispute, no opposition, no unequal mind. Their minds are even, kindly, loving, soft, gentle, workable, clear with faith, steady, free of hindrances, unshaken, untroubled; their minds practice the conduct of the perfection of wisdom. They have entered the understanding that is the mind’s support; they are like the ocean in wisdom and like Mount Sumeru in understanding, heaped with many good qualities. They play with the music of the factors of awakening and devote themselves to the music of the Buddha. They purify the eye of flesh and bring forth the divine eye;

they have arrived at the eye of wisdom and gone to the far shore of the eye of the Dharma; they bring the eye of a buddha to completion, teaching it, making it shine and explaining it in detail. They bring forth unobstructed knowledge; they are devoted to the sameness of the three realms; their minds are tamed and calm; they have the realization that no thing is found. They are skilled in explaining origination, possessed of the explanation of the Dharma, skilled in taking up and setting aside, skilled in what is reasonable and unreasonable. They live without interest in worldly talk; they find the essence in talk that goes beyond the world. They are skilled in seeking all things; they dwell in the knowledge that the nature of all things is stilled; their sphere is not-finding; they own nothing, grasp nothing, worry about nothing, are troubled by nothing; they are well freed without grasping; they are without blemish; they do not stay at any limit; they do not stay rooted even in the higher knowledges; their minds are unattached and do not shrink; devoted to the profound teachings, they do not sink.

They have entered and risen through the knowledge of a buddha, hard to understand; they have reached the path to the one destination; they are free of doubt, have crossed beyond uncertainty, have knowledge that depends on no one else, and are without conceit. In knowledge they rise high like Mount Sumeru; in understanding they are unshakable like the ocean; they surpass the light of the moon and sun with their wisdom and their pure, bright, lovely minds; they excel in good qualities that shine like refined gold. They are like the earth, because they bear the good and bad of all beings; like water, because they wash away the stains of all afflictions; like the king of fire, because they burn up the afflictions of conceit about all things; like the wind, because they cling to nothing in the world; like space, because they penetrate all things and own nothing at all.

They are like the lotus, because nothing in the world stains them; like a great cloud that comes in season, because they thunder the Dharma; like a great rain, because they shower the water of the Dharma; like a bull, because they surpass great crowds; like a great elephant, because their minds are supremely well tamed; like a noble thoroughbred horse, because they are well trained; like the lion, king of beasts, because they are courageous, confident and unafraid; like the banyan, king of trees, because they shelter all beings; like Sumeru, king of mountains, because no opponent can shake them; like the sky, because they cultivate measureless kindness; like the Great Brahma, because they lead the way in mastery of all roots of goodness and good things; like birds, because they store nothing up; like the garuda, king of birds, because they destroy the opponents’ arguments; like the udumbara flower, because their appearance is rare and sought after. Like great elephants they are well collected, undistracted, their faculties straight; they are skilled in judging, rich in patience and gentleness, free of envy because they do not covet the success of others.

They are confident in talks on the Dharma; never satisfied in seeking the Dharma; like beryl in morality; mines of jewels in learning; sweet-voiced with the sound of the great drum of the Dharma. They beat the great drum of the Dharma, blow the great conch of the Dharma, raise the great banner of the Dharma, light the great torch of the Dharma. They see with wisdom; they are unconfused, faultless, their rancor stilled, pure, without the smell of decay, without greed. They delight in sharing, give freely with open hands, delight in giving and sharing both the Dharma and material things, are not stingy in giving, are unentangled, their minds unafraid. They are dispassionate, steadfast, heroic, able to bear the burden, resolute, with a sense of shame, beyond compare, unhindered; they have gained the higher knowledges; they are kind and easy to live with, doers of good, lamps of the world, leaders. They have abandoned delight, passion, attachment and aversion; they are pure, free of sorrow, stainless, rid of the three stains; they play with the higher knowledges; they have the power of their causes and the power of their vows; they are straight and not crooked.

They have planted roots of goodness under many hundreds of thousands of kotis of nayutas of buddhas; they have pulled out the dart of pride; they are free of passion, hatred and delusion; pure, pure in conviction, praised by the excellent victors, wise in the ways of the world, risen through refined knowledge, extolled by the victors, uplifted in mind; heroic, firm, unequaled, without rancor, incomparable, dustless, harmonious, noble, bulls among men; with a sense of shame, resolute, mindful, intelligent, understanding, wielding the sword of wisdom, meritorious, radiant, rid of rancor and stain, devoted to the lasting truths. Such, Ananda, in brief, are the bodhisattvas, the great beings, in that buddha-field. But if the Tathagata were to describe them in detail, even with a lifespan lasting hundreds of thousands of kotis of nayutas of eons, he could not reach the end of the good qualities of those good men.

And yet the Tathagata’s confidence would not be cut off. Why? Because, Ananda, both of these are beyond thought and beyond compare: the good qualities of those bodhisattvas, and the unsurpassed wisdom and eloquence of the Tathagata.

And now, Ananda, rise, face west, scatter flowers, join your palms and bow down. That is the direction where that Blessed One, the Tathagata Amitabha, the arhat, the perfectly awakened one, is living, dwelling and carrying on, and teaching the Dharma: dustless and pure, whose name sounds unobstructed through the worlds of the ten directions, whom buddhas, blessed ones, as many as the sands of the Ganges in each direction praise, extol and laud again and again, with unobstructed speech that none can answer.” When this was said, the venerable Ananda said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, I want to see that Tathagata Amitabha, Boundless Light, Boundless Radiance, Boundless Life, the arhat, the perfectly awakened one, and those bodhisattvas, great beings, who have planted roots of goodness under many hundreds of thousands of kotis of nayutas of buddhas.”

The moment the venerable Ananda had said this, that Tathagata Amitabha, the arhat, the perfectly awakened one, sent out from the palm of his hand such a light that this buddha-field, a hundred thousand kotis of fields away, was filled with a great radiance. At that time, everywhere in those hundred thousand kotis of buddha-fields, all the black mountains and jewel mountains, Meru and Great Meru, Muchilinda and Great Muchilinda, Chakravada and Great Chakravada, walls and pillars, thickets of trees, gardens and palaces, heavenly and human, were pierced through and outshone by that light of the Tathagata.

Just as, when the sun has risen, a man standing a fathom away can see another man, so at that moment the monks, nuns, laymen and laywomen in this buddha-field, and the gods, nagas, yakshas, gandharvas, asuras, garudas, kinnaras and mahoragas, saw that Tathagata Amitabha, the arhat, the perfectly awakened one, risen above all fields like Sumeru, king of mountains, outshining every direction, shining, blazing, glowing and gleaming; and they saw that great host of bodhisattvas and that community of monks; all through the Buddha’s power, because that light was so pure.

Just as, if this great earth were to become one sheet of water, no trees, mountains, islands, grass, bushes, herbs or plants, no rivers, chasms or waterfalls could be made out; there would be only the great earth turned into a single ocean: in the same way, in that buddha-field there was no other sign or mark to be seen except the disciples with a light of a fathom, the bodhisattvas with a light of a hundred thousand kotis of leagues, and that Blessed One, the Tathagata Amitabha, the arhat, the perfectly awakened one, outshining that host of disciples and that host of bodhisattvas, lighting up every direction.

At that time, the bodhisattvas, disciples, gods and humans in that world Sukhavati all saw this world, and the Tathagata Shakyamuni surrounded by a great community of monks, teaching the Dharma. Then the Blessed One said to the bodhisattva, the great being Ajita (Maitreya): “Ajita, do you see the perfection of the splendid array and adornment of good qualities in that buddha-field? Above, in the sky, delightful parks, delightful groves, delightful gardens, delightful rivers and lotus ponds, strewn with blue, red, white and other lotuses and water lilies made of many jewels; and below, from the surface of the ground up to the abode of the Akanishtha gods, the sky strewn with flowers, adorned with garlands of flowers, filled with rows of many pillars, and visited by flocks of many birds conjured up by the Tathagata?”

He said: “I see it, Blessed One.” The Blessed One said: “And do you see, Ajita, these other flocks of birds that make all buddha-fields hear with the voice of a buddha, so that these bodhisattvas are never apart from recollecting the Buddha?” He said: “I see them, Blessed One.” The Blessed One said: “Do you see, Ajita, those beings in that buddha-field who have climbed into palaces a hundred thousand leagues across and move freely through the sky?” He said: “I see them, Blessed One.” The Blessed One said: “What do you think, Ajita: is there any difference between the gods who wield power over others’ creations and the humans in the world Sukhavati?” He said: “Blessed One, I do not see a single difference. That is how great the powers of the humans in this world Sukhavati are.”

The Blessed One said: “And do you see, Ajita, some people in that world Sukhavati dwelling in a womb inside great lotuses?” He said: “Blessed One, just as the gods of the Thirty-Three or the Yama gods enter palaces fifty leagues, a hundred leagues or five hundred leagues across and play, delight and enjoy themselves, so, Blessed One, I see some people in this world Sukhavati dwelling in a womb inside great lotuses. And there are beings here, Blessed One, who are born spontaneously, appearing seated cross-legged in lotuses. What is the cause here, Blessed One, what is the reason, that some live in a womb while others are born spontaneously, appearing seated cross-legged in lotuses?”

cmp.note: 「住在胎中」与「化生」。这一段是净土经里著名的「胎生与化生」：心怀疑惑的人虽然往生，却在莲花中像住在胎里一样，一段时间见不到佛；信心无疑的人直接化生在莲花上。康僧铠本说胎生者「五百岁中常不见佛」，梵本下文同样以五百年为期。
cmp.en: “Dwelling in a womb” and “born spontaneously.” This is the well-known passage on “womb birth and spontaneous birth” in the Pure Land sutras: those reborn there with doubts dwell inside the lotus as if in a womb and for a time cannot see the Buddha, while those with undoubting faith are born directly, seated on the lotus. Kang Sengkai says the womb-born “do not see the Buddha for five hundred years,” and the Sanskrit below gives the same five-hundred-year span.

verses.en: The Blessed One said: “Ajita, those bodhisattvas living in other buddha-fields who have doubts about being reborn in the world Sukhavati, and plant roots of goodness with that state of mind, dwell in a womb here. But those who are free of doubt and have cut off uncertainty, who plant roots of goodness for rebirth in the world Sukhavati, and who trust, have faith in and are convinced of the unobstructed knowledge of the buddhas, the blessed ones, are born there spontaneously, appearing seated cross-legged in lotuses.

Ajita, those bodhisattvas, great beings, living in other buddha-fields, who raise the thought of seeing the Tathagata Amitabha, the arhat, the perfectly awakened one, who have no doubt, who do not question the unobstructed knowledge of a buddha, and who have faith in their own roots of goodness: when they are born spontaneously, appearing seated cross-legged in lotuses, in just a moment their bodies become like those of other beings who were born there long ago. See, Ajita, the weakness of wisdom, the unevenness of wisdom, the loss of wisdom, the smallness of wisdom: for five hundred years they lose the sight of the Buddha, the sight of the bodhisattvas, the sight of the true Dharma, and discussion of the Dharma; they lose the practice of roots of goodness and the success of all roots of goodness; all because of notions and attention that have fallen into doubt.

Ajita, it is like this: suppose a consecrated kshatriya king had a prison inlaid all over with gold and beryl, hung with silk ribbons, garlands and clusters of flowers, spread with canopies of many colors, covered with fine cloths, strewn with many pearls and flowers, spacious, perfumed with incense, adorned with towers, mansions, windows, railings and gateways and every kind of jewel, covered with nets of gold, jewels and bangles, four-sided, with four pillars, four doors and four stairways. And suppose the king’s son, for some reason, were thrown into it and bound with fetters made of Jambu-river gold. And a couch were set out for him there, spread with many woolen rugs, spread with cotton and straw mattresses, as soft to the touch as kachalindika cloth, covered with a Kalinga coverlet with an upper sheet, with red pillows at both ends, bright and lovely to look at.

He might sit or lie on it, and plenty of pure, fine food and drink of many kinds might be brought to him there. What do you think, Ajita: would that prince’s enjoyment be rich?” He said: “Rich, Blessed One.” The Blessed One said: “What do you think, Ajita: would he taste it, savor it, or find contentment in it?” He said: “No indeed, Blessed One. Rather, he would long only to get out, because the king, displeased with him, had thrown him into that prison. He would seek out noble princes, ministers, the women of the palace, merchant bankers, householders or local rulers who might free him from that prison. Blessed One, the prince has no delight in that prison, and he is not freed from it until the king shows him favor.”

cmp.note: 「牢房」：用一座黄金宝石打造、什么都不缺的牢房，比喻因疑惑而「胎生」的人：舒适，却出不去、见不到佛。康僧铠本也用了这个「转轮王子坐罪、金锁系之」的比喻。英文、白话都照梵文详细译出所有陈设，因为比喻的力量正在于「什么都好，唯独没有自由」。
cmp.en: “A prison”: a prison built of gold and jewels and lacking nothing is the image for those “born in a womb” because of doubt: comfortable, yet unable to get out or see the Buddha. Kang Sengkai uses the same image of a prince who has offended and is bound with golden chains. The English and the plain Chinese translate every furnishing in the Sanskrit, because the image’s force lies in “everything is fine, except that there is no freedom.”

verses.en: The Blessed One said: “In the same way, Ajita, those bodhisattvas who have fallen into doubt and plant roots of goodness, who question the knowledge of a buddha, the knowledge equal to the unequaled: though they are reborn here in the world Sukhavati simply through hearing the Buddha’s name and that bit of faith in their minds, they are not born spontaneously, appearing seated cross-legged in lotuses; rather, they dwell in a womb inside the lotuses. Though they there have the sense of gardens and palaces, though there is no excrement or urine, no spittle or snot, and nothing unpleasant occurs to the mind, still for five hundred years they are separated from seeing the Buddha, hearing the Dharma, seeing the bodhisattvas, discussing and settling the Dharma, and all practice of wholesome things. So they take no delight there and find no contentment.

But when they have worked off their earlier fault, they come out of there afterward. And when they come out, it cannot be made out whether they come out above, below or to the side. See, Ajita: in those five hundred years they could have attended on many hundreds of thousands of kotis of nayutas of buddhas, planted many countless, measureless roots of goodness, and taken up the qualities of a buddha; and they lose all of it through the fault of doubt. See, Ajita, what great harm doubt brings to bodhisattvas.

Therefore, Ajita, bodhisattvas should be free of doubt, raise the mind toward awakening, and, in order to gain quickly the ability to bring good and happiness to all beings, dedicate their roots of goodness to rebirth in the world Sukhavati, where the Blessed One, the Tathagata Amitayus, the arhat, the perfectly awakened one, is.” When this was said, the bodhisattva Ajita said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how many mature bodhisattvas from this buddha-field, or from the presence of other buddhas, blessed ones, will be reborn in the world Sukhavati?” The Blessed One said: “Ajita, from this buddha-field seventy-two kotis of nayutas of mature bodhisattvas will be reborn in the world Sukhavati, mature and irreversible, with roots of goodness planted under many hundreds of thousands of kotis of buddhas.

Let alone those with smaller roots of goodness. From the presence of the Tathagata Dushprasaha, eighteen kotis of nayutas of bodhisattvas will be reborn in the world Sukhavati. In the eastern direction lives a Tathagata named Ratnakara;

from his presence ninety kotis of bodhisattvas will be reborn in the world Sukhavati. From the presence of the Tathagata Jyotishprabha, twenty-two kotis of bodhisattvas will be reborn in the world Sukhavati. From the presence of the Tathagata Amitaprabha, twenty-five kotis of bodhisattvas will be reborn in the world Sukhavati. From the presence of the Tathagata Lokapradipa, sixty kotis of bodhisattvas will be reborn in the world Sukhavati. From the presence of the Tathagata Nagabhibhu, sixty-four kotis of bodhisattvas will be reborn in the world Sukhavati. From the presence of the Tathagata Virajaprabha, twenty-five kotis of bodhisattvas will be reborn in the world Sukhavati. From the presence of the Tathagata Simha, eighteen thousand bodhisattvas will be reborn in the world Sukhavati. From the presence of the Tathagata Shrikuta, eighty-one kotis of nayutas of bodhisattvas will be reborn in the world Sukhavati. From the presence of the Tathagata Narendraraja, ten kotis of nayutas of bodhisattvas will be reborn in the world Sukhavati. From the presence of the Tathagata Balabhijna, twelve thousand bodhisattvas will be reborn in the world Sukhavati. From the presence of the Tathagata Pushpadhvaja, twenty-five kotis of bodhisattvas who have attained vigor, setting out together as one, will in a single week put ninety-nine hundred thousand kotis of nayutas of eons behind them and be reborn in the world Sukhavati. From the presence of the Tathagata Jvalanadhipati, twelve kotis of bodhisattvas will be reborn in the world Sukhavati. From the presence of the Tathagata Vaisharadyaprapta, sixty-nine kotis of bodhisattvas will be reborn in the world Sukhavati: to see the Tathagata Amitabha, to bow to him, to attend on him, to ask him questions and to inquire of him.

In this way, Ajita, I could go on for a full koti of nayutas of eons naming those Tathagatas from whom bodhisattvas go to the world Sukhavati to see, bow to and attend on that Tathagata Amitabha, and still I could not reach the end. See, Ajita, what a great gain those beings have gained who will hear the name of the Tathagata Amitabha, the arhat, the perfectly awakened one. Those beings who gain even a single thought of faith in that Tathagata and in this teaching of the Dharma will not be of lowly inclination.

Therefore, Ajita, I tell you, I declare to you, before the world with its gods: to hear this teaching of the Dharma, even if one had to plunge into and cross a great galaxy of a billion worlds full of fire, one should not feel a single moment of regret. Why? Because, Ajita, kotis of bodhisattvas turn back from unsurpassed, perfect awakening through not hearing teachings of the Dharma like this. Therefore one should make a very great effort, with deep resolve, to hear, take up and hold this teaching of the Dharma, to master it, to explain it at length, and to cultivate it.

Even for a single day and night, even for just the time it takes to milk a cow, one should write it out well, even in the form of a book, and keep it, and regard it as the Teacher; if one wishes to establish measureless beings quickly and irreversibly in unsurpassed, perfect awakening, to see the buddha-field of that Blessed One, the Tathagata Amitabha, and to take up for oneself a special perfection of the splendid array and adornment of good qualities of a buddha-field.

But, Ajita, those beings will have gained an exceedingly great gain, will have planted roots of goodness, will have served the victors of the past and been upheld by the power of the buddhas, within whose hearing noble teachings of the Dharma like these will come in the future, even when the true Dharma is disappearing: teachings praised by all the buddhas, extolled by all the buddhas, approved by all the buddhas, which quickly bring the great knowledge of all-knowing. Having heard them, they will gain a noble joy and gladness; they will take them up, hold them, recite them, master them and explain them at length to others; they will delight in cultivating them; they will even write them out and worship them; and they will produce so much merit that it is not easy to count. So, Ajita, what had to be done by a Tathagata, I have done.

Now you must practice free of doubt. Do not question that unobstructed, unhindered knowledge of a buddha. Do not end up entering the prison of a jeweled lotus provided with everything. For, Ajita, the appearance of a buddha is rare, the teaching of the Dharma is rare, the right moment is rare. Ajita, I have told you how the perfection of former roots of goodness is attained. Now you must apply yourselves and practice. Ajita, I make a great entrusting of this teaching of the Dharma so that it will not be lost. Do not strive for the disappearance of the qualities of a buddha. Do not disturb the Tathagata’s command.”

Then, at that moment, the Blessed One spoke these verses: “Those who have not made merit will not hear teachings like these; but those heroes who have reached their goal will hear these words. (1) Those who have seen the perfectly awakened one, the lord of the world, the maker of light, and heard the Dharma with reverence, will gain the highest joy. (2) The lowly, the lazy, those with wrong views cannot find faith in the teachings of the buddhas. Those who worshipped the buddhas of the past have trained in the conduct of the lords of the world. (3) Just as a man without eyes in the dark does not know the way, so how could he show it? Just so all the disciples are ignorant of a buddha’s knowledge, let alone other beings. (4) Only a buddha knows the good qualities of a buddha; not gods, nagas, asuras, yakshas or disciples.

What way in is there even for solitary buddhas when the knowledge of a buddha is being made known? (5) If all beings became Sugatas, with pure knowledge and supreme skill, and for kotis of eons or longer they told the good qualities of a single buddha, (6) they would pass into nirvana in the meantime, after telling them for many kotis of eons, and still the measure of a buddha’s knowledge would not be found: such is the knowledge and practice of the victors. (7) So a wise and discerning person who trusts my words is a witness to the whole mass of the victors’ knowledge: a buddha knows, and would speak, the word. (8) Only now and then is a human birth gained, only now and then do buddhas appear;

faith and wisdom are gained only after a very long time; so let those who understand the meaning make an effort. (9) Those who, hearing such a Dharma, gain the highest joy remembering the Sugata, were our friends in times past; they are buddhas who raise the resolve for awakening.” (10) While the Blessed One was speaking this teaching of the Dharma, the Dharma-eye, dustless and stainless, became pure regarding things in twelve kotis of nayutas of beings; twenty-four kotis reached the fruit of non-returning; the minds of eight hundred monks were freed from the outflows, no longer grasping; and twenty-five kotis of bodhisattvas gained the acceptance that things are unborn.

And in forty hundred thousand kotis of nayutas of gods and humans, minds that had never arisen before were raised toward unsurpassed, perfect awakening, and they planted roots of goodness for rebirth in Sukhavati, wishing to see the Blessed One Amitabha. All of them, having been born there, will in due course be reborn in other worlds as Tathagatas, all named Manjusvara (“Sweet Voice”). And eighty kotis of nayutas who had gained acceptance from the Tathagata Dipamkara and were irreversible from unsurpassed, perfect awakening, who had been brought to maturity by that very Tathagata Amitayus while he was carrying out his former bodhisattva practice, will be reborn in the world Sukhavati and fulfill the practice of their former vows. And at that moment this great galaxy of a billion worlds shook in six ways;

various miracles appeared; the ground was strewn knee-deep with mandarava flowers; heavenly and human instruments played; and the sound of rejoicing was heard up to the abode of the Akanishtha gods. This is what the Blessed One said. Delighted, the bodhisattva, the great being Ajita, the venerable Ananda, that whole assembly, and the world with its gods, humans, asuras and gandharvas rejoiced at what the Blessed One had said. The proclaiming of the good qualities of the Blessed One Amitabha; the bodhisattvas’ entry into the stage of no turning back. Here ends the chapter on Amitabha’s array of Sukhavati.
